The 3 Day Reset

Twenty seven swaps, three days, easiest first.

Nobody does twenty seven things at once, so this is split by what each one asks of you rather than by how important it sounds.

The next page is four routes: heat, contact time, dust and water. Read it and the rest of the guide stops being a list to memorise, because every swap after it is one of those four.

Day one is nine habits and nothing to buy. Day two swaps nine everyday products as they run out, so your shopping list changes and your spending does not. Day three is nine purchases that last years.

Do not throw anything out. Replacing a full cupboard in one weekend is how people quit. Let things run out.

Each day also has one thing to add at the table, because everything else here is a removal and a list of removals is a miserable way to spend three days.

Before the list

How this actually gets in

An endocrine disruptor is a chemical that can interfere with hormone signalling, because its shape is close enough to one of your own hormones that the body's receptors respond to it. That is the whole idea. What makes it worth three days of your attention is not any single product. It is that four ordinary routes repeat all day, every day, and those same four explain nearly every swap on the pages that follow.

  • Heat

    Heat is the biggest multiplier in this guide. Plastic is a solid holding smaller molecules loosely inside it, and warming it loosens that grip, so more of what is in the plastic moves into whatever the plastic is touching. Oily and fatty food pulls across more than water does. That one mechanism is the microwave, the bottom rack of the dishwasher, the bottle left in a hot car, the cling film over a warm bowl and the scratched pan on a high flame. It is why day one starts where it does.

  • Skin, and how long it stays on

    Skin is not a seal. What matters is contact time and surface area rather than how strong something smells: a detergent stays in the fabric against you for the next sixteen hours, and a body wash covers all of you at once. This is why the guide goes after the things you use every day without thinking, the hand soap and the shampoo and the laundry powder, and leaves the perfume you wear once a month alone. Frequency beats intensity nearly every time.

  • House dust

    Furniture foam, electronics casings, vinyl flooring and carpet shed slowly for years, and what they shed collects in dust. Dust is not a housekeeping problem here, it is the delivery route: it settles, it gets walked through, it goes back up into the air, and it is breathed and swallowed. Small children get the most of it, because they are lower down and their hands go in their mouths. Damp cloths, shoes at the door and a sealed vacuum are three versions of the same fix.

  • Water, drunk and breathed

    Some of what is in tap water is regulated and reported, which is why a water report is worth reading and why this guide has a page on how. The part people miss is that a hot shower turns some of it into vapour in a small closed room, so water is an inhaled exposure and not only a swallowed one. That is why day three lists two filters rather than one, and why day one leaves the extractor fan running.

None of these are exotic. Heat, contact time, dust and water. Once you can see which one a swap is about, you can work out the rest of your house on your own.

Day 1 of 3

Nothing to buy. Do it today.

Nine habits. No shopping, no research, nothing to order.

  • Never heat food in plastic

    Not the microwave, and not hot leftovers going straight into a container. Heat is what makes plastic give up what is in it, and fat pulls across more than water does, so a curry is a worse case than a soup. This is the single highest yield habit in the guide because it costs nothing and it happens daily. Plate first, container after it cools.

  • Say no to the receipt

    Thermal receipt paper is usually coated with BPA or BPS and it transfers to your fingers. Take the emailed copy where it is offered, and wash your hands when you have to handle one. If you handle receipts all day at work, this one matters more for you than for most people.

  • Damp dust, and open a window for ten minutes

    Household dust is where the plasticizers and flame retardants from furniture and electronics end up, and a closed room concentrates what is already in it. Use a damp cloth. A dry duster mostly moves it around.

  • Shoes off at the door

    Outdoor dust, road residue and lawn treatments come in on the soles of shoes and end up in the carpet where they get walked back into the air. This one costs nothing and it halves how much dusting the last swap needs.

  • Keep plastic out of the dishwasher

    The bottom rack is the hottest part of the machine and hot detergent is abrasive. Between the heat and the wear, dishwasher cycles are what turn a smooth container cloudy, and a degraded surface sheds more than a new one. Hand wash, or replace it on day three.

  • Do not leave drinks sitting in a hot car

    A bottle on the passenger seat in July is the same mechanism as the microwave, only slower: heat plus time, and a parked car in the sun runs far hotter than the day outside it. The taste of that water afterwards is the mechanism telling on itself. Take it inside, or carry the steel bottle from day three.

  • Air the car for a minute before you drive

    A hot car is a sealed plastic box, and that new car smell is the interior off gassing into the air you are about to breathe for an hour. Crack the windows for a minute before you get in, especially in summer. It costs nothing.

  • Run the extractor fan while you shower, and after

    A bathroom in use is a small closed room full of hot water vapour and whatever is in your products. The fan is already there. Leave it running for ten minutes after you get out.

  • Wash new clothes before you wear them

    New fabric carries the finishes it was treated with in the factory, sizing and softeners and anti wrinkle coatings, and the first wash takes most of that off. It matters most for anything that sits against skin all day and for anything a child sleeps in. One wash, once, and then you never have to think about it again.

At the table

At the table: cruciferous vegetables

One serving today of broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, kale or rocket. This family contains compounds called glucosinolates, which are actively studied for their role in how the liver processes what passes through it. Nothing needs to come out of a bottle. A side of broccoli counts.

Easiest version: roast a tray of whatever is cheapest, eat some tonight, keep the rest for tomorrow.

Day 2 of 3

Replace only as they run out.

Same shopping list, different items on it. Nothing extra to spend.

  • Laundry detergent and dryer sheets

    This is the highest contact time of anything you own: whatever is in it sits against your skin for the next sixteen hours and goes into the air of the whole house. Unscented detergent, and wool balls instead of sheets.

  • Deodorant, body wash and shampoo

    Every day, large surface area, straight onto skin. Read the ingredient list rather than the word on the front. Fragrance is the one to watch: on a label it is a catch-all that does not have to list what is inside it, and phthalates are commonly in there.

  • Candles, plug-ins and air freshener

    Do not swap these for a nicer scented version, because the scent is the thing being released. A plug-in is a device whose entire job is to put a fragrance mixture into the air of a closed room continuously, and on a label the word fragrance covers a mixture that does not have to be itemised. If you want the room to smell like something, open a window or simmer citrus peel.

  • Dish soap and all purpose cleaner

    These go onto the surfaces your food touches, and into the air of the room you stand in longest. Fragrance free is the whole swap, and it is not a specialist purchase: most supermarkets carry an unscented line at the ordinary price, usually beside the one you buy now.

  • Hand soap

    The most used product in the house, and the one nobody thinks about because it is on the skin for ten seconds. Ten seconds, twelve times a day, every day, is more total contact than the thing you use once a week for ten minutes. Contact time is the whole argument, and fragrance free is usually the cheaper bottle anyway.

  • Cling film and sandwich bags

    Both meet food directly and cling film usually meets it warm, which is the heat route on the smallest possible scale and the highest possible frequency. Beeswax wraps, paper, or a plate over the bowl. The bags are the easy half, because the containers that replace them are already in your cupboard.

  • Anything scented in your makeup bag

    Perfume, scented moisturiser, body spray, hair oil. Same rule as the shower: the word fragrance covers a mixture that does not have to be listed. Start with whatever you use daily and leave the once a month things alone.

  • Nail polish and remover

    Polish is one of the few products where the ingredients of concern are named on the bottle, so this swap is easy to shop for. Look for the ones that say they leave out toluene, formaldehyde and dibutyl phthalate. Do it in a room with a window open.

  • Cleaning wipes and baby wipes

    A wipe is a fragranced solution held against skin or a food surface, with no rinse step. A damp cloth does the same job for nothing, and where you want a wipe, buy the fragrance free version.

At the table

At the table: fibre

Beans, lentils, oats, berries, leafy greens. Fibre is the part of food that is not absorbed, and it is what carries material out through the gut rather than leaving it to sit. Most people eat around half of what the national guidelines recommend, which makes this the easiest gap in the list to close.

Easiest version: a tin of beans into whatever you were cooking anyway, and swap one refined thing for a wholegrain one.

Day 3 of 3

Buy once, keep for years.

The only day that costs money. Nine purchases, spread over as long as you like.

  • A water filter for drinking water

    Buy this by its certification rather than its brand. NSF/ANSI 53 covers lead, 58 is reverse osmosis and the one that addresses PFAS, and 42 is taste and odour only, which is the cheap pitcher most people already own and the reason they think they are covered. A carbon pitcher carrying 53 is a real improvement; under sink reverse osmosis is the serious version. If you buy one thing on this page, buy this, because you drink it every day and you do not get to choose your supply.

  • A shower filter

    Hot water in a closed room means you breathe what is in your water rather than only drinking it, and a ten minute shower with the door shut is ten minutes of exactly that. A shower filter is a different fitting from a drinking filter and neither one does the other's job. It screws onto the arm in about a minute, costs less than most things on this page, and almost nobody has one.

  • One good pan

    Cast iron or stainless. Nonstick is a surface layer, and heat and scratches are what break that layer down, which is the point at which the pan starts leaving some of itself in the food instead of on the pan. An old scratched pan over a high flame is the worst case in most kitchens, so that is the one to replace first. You do not need a set. You need the one you actually cook in most days.

  • Glass or steel for food storage

    Start with whatever holds your leftovers, because that is the container that meets heat twice: hot food goes into it, and it comes back out of a microwave. Cold storage is a far smaller deal, so the salad box can wait until it wears out. Glass costs more once and then never needs replacing, which is most of why it works out cheaper.

  • A steel or glass water bottle

    The bottle you refill every day and leave in the car gets more heat and more wear than anything else you drink from, and a scuffed surface sheds more than a smooth one. It is also the highest contact time on this page, because you put it to your mouth thirty times a day without noticing. Steel does not care about heat, scratches or time.

  • Wooden or steel cooking utensils

    Black plastic spatulas and spoons are designed to sit in a hot pan, which is the exact condition that gets things out of plastic fastest, and they are usually the cheapest plastic in the kitchen. The tell is a melted or warped edge: that utensil has already been past its limit repeatedly. Wood or steel costs a few pounds, lasts a decade, and cannot melt into dinner.

  • A vacuum with a real HEPA filter

    This is what makes day one's dusting worth doing. Dust is where the flame retardants and plasticizers from furniture and electronics collect, and a vacuum without a sealed filter lifts the fine fraction and returns it to the room through the exhaust. The fine fraction is the part light enough to hang in the air long enough to breathe, so a leaky vacuum is close to a redistribution machine. Look for sealed, not only for the word HEPA on the box.

  • Plain cotton or linen bedding

    Eight hours a night, whole body, face down in it and breathing it, which is the longest single stretch of contact anywhere in your house. The thing to avoid is the finish rather than the fabric: wrinkle free, stain resistant and permanent press are all coatings applied to cloth, and some wrinkle free finishes are formaldehyde based. Untreated and undyed on the label beats any claim on the front of the pack.

  • A HEPA air purifier for the bedroom

    Last on the list on purpose. It is the most expensive thing here and it does the least on its own, because it treats the air rather than the source, and everything above it removes a source. In a bedroom you genuinely cannot ventilate, an internal room or a city window you will not open at night, it earns its place. If you can open a window instead, open the window.

At the table

At the table: protein and sulphur foods

Eggs, fish, onions, garlic, leeks. Sulphur containing foods are studied for their part in the liver pathways that process what the body needs to clear, and eating enough protein is what those pathways are built from. There is nothing to buy and no amount to hit here. It is a normal plate.

Easiest version: put protein at breakfast, where most people skip it, and cook with onion and garlic as a default.

If you pulled your water report

Reading your water report

Two numbers do most of the work on a water report, and neither means what people assume. This page is how to read yours.

  • What the lead number means

    Utilities report lead as a 90th percentile: nine of the ten homes they sampled were at or below that number. The federal action level is 15 parts per billion, and that is the point at which the utility has to act, not a line between safe and unsafe. The EPA's health based goal for lead is zero. Your own tap can sit either side of the system figure, because most lead comes from the pipe and fittings between the main and your kitchen rather than from the treatment plant.

  • What the PFAS number means

    PFAS are a family of thousands of manufactured compounds. In 2024 the EPA set enforceable limits for six of them, including 4 parts per trillion for PFOA and for PFOS. A count of detections tells you how many were found above the reporting limit, not how much of each. If your report says the system was not sampled, that is an absence of data and not an absence of PFAS: it usually means the system was too small to be in the monitoring round.

  • Which filter takes out what

    Filters are certified against numbered standards, and the number on the box is what to look for rather than the brand. NSF/ANSI 53 covers lead. NSF/ANSI 58 is reverse osmosis, the broadest coverage and the one that addresses PFAS. NSF/ANSI 42 is aesthetic only, chlorine and taste and odour, which is the cheapest and does nothing for lead or PFAS. NSF/ANSI 401 covers emerging contaminants including some pharmaceuticals. A pitcher carrying 42 on its own is doing less than most people assume it is.

  • The shower is a separate problem

    Day three lists a shower filter for a reason that a drinking water report does not cover. Hot water in a closed room means some of what is in the water leaves it as vapour, so the exposure route is what you breathe rather than what you drink. A shower filter is a different fitting from a drinking filter and neither replaces the other.

Straight with you

This is not medical advice and none of it is a diagnosis. If you are being treated for a hormone condition, run changes past your doctor first. The research here is still developing and honest people disagree about how much any single exposure matters. What is not really in dispute is that daily beats occasional, and that most of what is on these pages costs little or nothing and is hard to regret.
